title: Comtech and U.S. Marine Corps Establish Longest Ever Low Power Troposcatter Link in Hawaii
summary: Record 187-Mile Comtech COMET MPR troposcatter link successfully connects Pearl...
body_markdown:
*Record 187-Mile Comtech COMET MPR troposcatter link successfully connects Pearl Harbor and Pohakuloa Training Area during first-of-its-kind exercise.*


CHANDLER, Ariz. –


November 18, 2026– **** Comtech Telecommunications Corp. (NASDAQ: CMTL) (“Comtech” or the “Company”), a global communications technology leader, today announced that during Tropo Thunder, a first-of-its-kind U.S. Marine Corps demonstration in Hawaii, the company’s[Comtech COMET MPR](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=https%3A%2F%2Fcomtech.com%2Fcapability%2Fmpr-platform%2F&esheet=54643223&newsitemid=20261117996696&lan=en-US&anchor=Comtech+COMET+MPR&index=1&md5=643f59b700a0b098f772bd89e862597f) (MPR) showcased a small team, rapidly deployable terrestrial Beyond Line-of-Sight (BLOS) communications capability in a geographically challenging environment, successfully establishing the longest low power troposcatter link ever recorded by the U.S. Marine Corps.


The Comtech COMET MPR paired with a 2.4 m inflatable antenna at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii.


Comtech’s MPR delivers a unique, resilient communications link that keeps forces connected BLOS without the need for satellite or fiber infrastructure. The Tropo Thunder exercise didn’t merely showcase sending a radio signal 187 miles. It was demonstrated that communications traditionally associated with much larger equipment and infrastructure can be delivered in a package small enough to move with an expeditionary force.


Throughout the demonstration, the MPR link connected Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam on Oahu with Pohakuloa Training Area on Hawaii island, spanning 187 miles/301km. The link delivered an average throughput of approximately 10 Mbps, while maintaining 100% availability and approximately 6ms of round-trip latency. The performance was achieved using low transmit power at each end of the link, demonstrating the ability of low power, expeditionary system to maintain high-quality BLOS communications across an extended overwater path.


“Exercise Tropo Thunder demonstrated just how far modern troposcatter communications have advanced,” said Mark Yamamoto, Vice President of North America Solutions at Comtech. “Comtech’s market leadership in low power troposcatter technology is helping expeditionary forces maintain the connectivity and information advantage they need in today’s operational environments. We look forward to continuing to work with the U.S. Marine Corps to advance this critical technology and provide our men and women in uniform with the capabilities needed to stay ahead of near-peer threats.”


The exercise highlighted the MPR’s expeditionary characteristics. Each MPR radio and each 2.4-meter inflatable antenna can be transported in an airline-checkable case. The field configuration required approximately 30 minutes to deploy and operated with less than 350 watts of total prime power, significantly reducing the transportation, power, and infrastructure requirements traditionally associated with long-range terrestrial BLOS communications.


The MPR provides forces with an additional resilient BLOS communications pathway without requiring satellites or intermediate terrestrial infrastructure. Exercise Tropo Thunder demonstrated how this capability can support distributed and island-hopping operations by extending reliable connectivity between geographically separated locations.


The successful 187-mile link builds on Comtech’s continued work with the U.S. military to advance resilient BLOS communications and demonstrates the potential of low power, expeditionary troposcatter systems to keep forces connected across increasingly distributed and contested environments.
